title: How Gap and H&M implement AI for supply chain risk management
excerpt: Apparel brands like Target, H&M, and Gap use AI to enhance supply chain transparency and meet new sustainability regulations effectively.
content_html:
As the US and Europe tighten their supply chain regulations, apparel retailers face an urgent task: map and trace the many layers of their supply chains to gain full visibility into what's happening — not only at their direct suppliers, but also at their suppliers' suppliers.

Extended producer responsibility in the US and digital product passports in Europe — both of which are being implemented in phases over the coming months — require businesses to submit accurate documents to prove compliance with regulations, said Mark Burstein, the senior vice president for Americas at the software company Inspectorio, which provides an AI-powered supply chain management platform for retailers such as Gap and Mango.

Documentation could include factory audits, purchase orders, or records of water usage or carbon emissions throughout the supply chain, Burstein added.

"Everybody is fully loaded into moving forward with all of this traceability, because the regulations are coming up," Burstein said.

It's a key reason Burstein sees growing interest in AI within apparel supply chains, especially this year, he said. Manually providing documentation could take days or longer; AI is helping to shrink the process time to an hour.

Another reason, Burstein said, is that risk events such as the pandemic, sudden tariff increases, and geopolitical conflicts are becoming more frequent.

Brands like ASOS, H&M, and Gap are turning to AI platforms to unearth the complex layers of their supply chains, where sourcing, tariffs, water use, regulations, weather, and other factors impact how apparel is made and shipped.

"AI helps them bring the hidden risk to the surface a lot faster, before the disruption issue becomes a larger operational problem," Kenchen Bharwani, a fashion consultant at Empire Apparel LLC, a wholesale company specializing in sourcing and managing off-price apparel, told Business Insider.

Spotting risks and delays with AI

Apparel supply chains can be challenging to trace because a single product may have dozens of components from around the world, Burstein said. For a seemingly simple shirt, cotton might be picked in Turkey, sent to China for milling, and cut and sewn in Vietnam before the final product is shipped to the US for sale — not to mention that tags, packaging, and buttons may all be sourced from different locations.

OMJ Clothing, a custom suit maker in Charlotte, North Carolina, sometimes sources from 10 factories at a time and often struggles to keep up with the complex process, said its CEO and cofounder, Brad Rhyne.

In March, Rhyne used the AI model Claude to develop a custom dashboard to trace factory orders and view their current status, creating "a single source of truth CRM," he said.

Before the dashboard, a customer would contact the business to ask about the order status. Only then would OMJ dig in and realize something up the supply chain was delayed, said Rhyne. Now, the CRM pulls factory data into the dashboard so OMJ can proactively see delays before a customer reaches out, and either pivot to find a replacement or update the customer.

"We're able to dig into it before it even becomes an issue," Rhyne said.

Large brands are also using AI traceability tools to spot problems like human rights violations and environmental risks and take "corrective action sooner rather than later," Bharwani said. Vera Bradley uses TrusTrace's AI to monitor Customs and Border Protection's risk databases and screen for forced labor, and Adidas uses the platform alongside the World Resources Institute's Aqueduct tool to identify mills in flood-prone regions, she said.

H&M has reported using AI to identify flood risks and factory closures in Bangladesh and scale back some production in the country. A press contact for H&M told Business Insider that the retailer uses AI to improve supply chain visibility, reduce waste, and help meet its sustainability goals.

Some of the biggest retailers are committed to transparency, Bharwani added. She works with liquidated merchandise and has clients like Target, which publishes its global factory list.

"It's thousands of suppliers that they work with, and it's so detailed," she said, adding that global fashion retailer ASOS, which she doesn't work directly with, has traced its supply chain with AI all the way to the farm level.

Still, this process is an outlier. "ASOS is just the one in a million that manages to get as far as that," Bharwani said. "I don't think a lot of other brands have yet."

Manual work gets automated

Forthcoming regulations will make it essential for apparel retailers to keep tabs on their supply chain to comply with new laws, said Bharwani. US states are implementing extended producer responsibility policies, which hold apparel brands accountable for their products' lifecycle, from production through to after the garment is worn. The challenge: each state's exact policies and deadlines differ.

The Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act, which came into force in the US in 2022, requires importers to provide documented proof that no forced labor was used. Burstein said retailers previously had their suppliers fill in spreadsheets to manage compliance, but brands have since realized it's "almost impossible to manage this manually," Burstein said.

For retailers selling in Europe, Digital Product Passport rules mandate that brands include a QR code-linked digital record that discloses a product's materials, sustainability data, and traceability information. Textiles are among the priority product groups listed in the organization's rulebook.

In a manual workflow, a brand would need to identify the individual regulations that apply to its product, organize data it's collected on the product, ask suppliers for anything that's missing, review the data for accuracy, and submit reports to regulatory agencies, Burstein said. That process can take at least 30 hours per purchase order.

With AI, agents build the chain of custody, collect documents, and create compliance reports for specific regulations — shrinking the process to about one hour, including human review, he added.

"It's literally manual work, hours and hours and hours, that we're eliminating here," Burstein said.

content_html_zh:
随着美国和欧洲收紧供应链监管，服装零售商面临着一项紧迫任务：绘制和追踪其供应链的各个层面，以全面了解正在发生的情况——不仅是直接供应商，还包括供应商的供应商。

软件公司 Inspectorio 的美洲高级副总裁马克·布尔斯坦 (Mark Burstein) 表示，美国的生产者延伸责任和欧洲的数字产品护照都将在未来几个月内分阶段实施，这两者都要求企业提交准确的文件以证明遵守法规。Inspectorio 为 Gap 和 Mango 等零售商提供人工智能驱动的供应链管理平台。

伯斯坦补充说，文件可能包括工厂审核、采购订单或整个供应链的用水或碳排放记录。

“每个人都全力以赴推进所有这些可追溯性，因为法规即将出台，”伯斯坦说。

他说，这是 Burstein 认为服装供应链中人工智能越来越感兴趣的一个关键原因，尤其是今年。 手动提供文档可能需要数天或更长时间；人工智能正在帮助将处理时间缩短到一个小时。

布尔斯坦表示，另一个原因是疫情、关税突然上调、地缘政治冲突等风险事件变得更加频繁。

ASOS、H&M 和 Gap 等品牌正在转向人工智能平台来挖掘其供应链的复杂层面，其中采购、关税、用水、法规、天气和其他因素影响服装的制造和运输方式。

Empire Apparel LLC（一家专门采购和管理低价服装的批发公司）的时尚顾问 Kenchen Bharwani 告诉《商业内幕》，“人工智能可以帮助他们更快地将隐藏的风险暴露出来，避免中断问题变成更大的运营问题。”

利用人工智能发现风险和延误

布尔斯坦说，追踪服装供应链可能具有挑战性，因为单一产品可能有来自世界各地的数十个组件。 对于一件看似简单的衬衫，棉花可能会在土耳其采摘，送往中国进行铣削，并在越南进行裁剪和缝制，然后将最终产品运往美国出售——更不用说标签、包装和纽扣都可能来自不同的地点。

位于北卡罗来纳州夏洛特的 OMJ Clothing 是一家定制西装制造商，其首席执行官兼联合创始人 Brad Rhyne 表示，有时会同时从 10 家工厂采购，并且常常难以跟上复杂的流程。

今年 3 月，Rhyne 使用 AI 模型 Claude 开发了一个自定义仪表板来跟踪工厂订单并查看其当前状态，创建“单一真实来源 CRM”，他说。

在使用仪表板之前，客户会联系企业询问订单状态。 莱恩说，只有到那时，OMJ 才会深入研究并意识到供应链上游的某些事情被延迟了。 现在，CRM 将工厂数据提取到仪表板中，以便 OMJ 可以在客户联系之前主动查看延迟情况，然后转向寻找替代者或更新客户信息。

“我们能够在它成为问题之前对其进行深入研究，”莱恩说。

巴尔瓦尼表示，大品牌还使用人工智能追溯工具来发现侵犯人权和环境风险等问题，并“宜早不宜迟”采取纠正措施。 她说，Vera Bradley 使用 TrusTrace 的人工智能来监控海关和边境保护局的风险数据库并筛查强迫劳动，而阿迪达斯则使用该平台与世界资源研究所的 Aqueduct 工具一起识别洪水易发地区的工厂。

H&M 报告称，利用人工智能来识别孟加拉国的洪水风险和工厂关闭，并缩减该国的部分生产。 H&M 的一位新闻联系人告诉《商业内幕》，该零售商利用人工智能来提高供应链可视性、减少浪费并帮助实现其可持续发展目标。

巴尔瓦尼补充说，一些最大的零售商致力于提高透明度。 她与清算商品打交道，拥有 Target 等客户，该公司发布了其全球工厂名单。

她说：“他们与数千家供应商合作，而且非常详细。”她补充说，她没有直接与之合作的全球时尚零售商 ASOS 已经利用人工智能追踪其供应链，一直到农场层面。

尽管如此，这个过程还是一个异常值。 巴尔瓦尼说：“ASOS 是能够做到这一点的百万分之一。” “我认为很多其他品牌还没有这样做。”

手动工作变得自动化

巴尔瓦尼表示，即将出台的法规将使服装零售商必须密切关注其供应链以遵守新法律。 美国各州正在实施延伸的生产者责任政策，要求服装品牌对其产品的生命周期（从生产到服装穿着后）负责。 挑战：每个州的具体政策和截止日期都不同。

2022 年在美国生效的《维吾尔强迫劳动预防法》要求进口商提供没有使用强迫劳动的书面证据。 伯斯坦表示，零售商之前让供应商填写电子表格来管理合规性，但品牌后来意识到“几乎不可能手动管理”。

对于在欧洲销售的零售商来说，数字产品护照规则要求品牌包含与二维码链接的数字记录，该记录公开产品的材料、可持续性数据和可追溯性信息。 纺织品是该组织规则手册中列出的优先产品组之一。

伯斯坦说，在手动工作流程中，品牌需要确定适用于其产品的各个法规，组织在产品上收集的数据，向供应商询问缺失的内容，审查数据的准确性，并向监管机构提交报告。 每个采购订单的该过程可能至少需要 30 个小时。

他补充说，借助人工智能，特工可以建立监管链、收集文件并根据特定法规创建合规报告，将流程缩短到大约一小时，其中包括人工审查。

伯斯坦说：“这实际上是体力劳动，我们在这里要消除大量的体力劳动。”
